paras: The lynching of Bob Sarver was the hanging of a young Black man by a mob near Franklin, Simpson County, Kentucky, on the night of Monday, March 6, 1882. Accused of attempting to rape a 16-year-old white girl, Sarver was taken from officers who were moving him by train and was hanged from a tree at the scene of the alleged attempt. A one-line Nashville dispatch carried the case to papers across the country, and three men were later reported arrested for the killing.

According to the reports, the alleged attempt took place on Friday, March 3, against a white girl of 16 whom the papers named variously as Ruly, Sina or Tennie Ruley, and Tennie Ruby. The Bourbon News of Millersburg, Kentucky, said Sarver hid in a thicket in the Pilot Knob neighborhood, six miles northwest of Franklin, seized the girl as she passed and threatened her with a knife until men cutting wood nearby came at her cries. He fled, and the Stark County Democrat reported that he was arrested on Monday. A Nashville report printed in the Copiah Signal described him as about 18 years old with 'a fair character in the neighborhood.'

Officers tried to get Sarver away by train, toward Bowling Green 'for safety' in one account and away 'from an indignant mob that was collecting' in another. On Monday night the mob caught up with them: the Stark County Democrat said a crowd stopped the train at Franklin, and the Bourbon News said men 'presenting revolvers, entered the car and took Sarver out.' The Copiah Signal put the mob at about 75 armed and mounted men.

The mob carried Sarver back to the spot of the alleged attempt and hanged him from a tree beside the road. The Copiah Signal's account said he was hanged with a small rope tied in a knot 'as if done by an expert,' with his feet almost touching the ground. That account placed the site about 20 miles from Franklin, while the Bourbon News placed the scene six miles northwest of town.

A coroner and jury went to the scene at 1 p.m. the next day, cut down the body and returned a verdict of death at the hands of unknown persons. About a week later, the Memphis Daily Appeal reported that three 'gentlemen' had been arrested for taking 'the negro Sarver from the hands of the officers at Franklin, to be mobbed,' were being guarded in the jailer's residence, and would be tried on Monday. The same item said that 'public sentiment seems to be in their favor.' No report of the trial or its outcome was found.

Most papers knew the case only through a Nashville dispatch of March 7, which gave Sarver's name, the charge and the girl's name in a single sentence. Papers from Washington and New York to Arizona, Dakota and Nevada printed it, often with the name garbled as Sawyer, Sawer or Carver. Its headlines ranged from the neutral 'A Colored Man Lynched' in the Evening Star and New-York Tribune to the Memphis Public Ledger's 'Served Him Right' and the Las Vegas Daily Gazette's 'Rape Fiend Lynched.' The Memphis Daily Appeal's headline is printed in the digitized text as 'Would-be Baptist Lynched.'

Fuller accounts appeared later in the week in regional papers. The Stark County Democrat of Canton, Ohio, called Sarver 'the fiend,' and the Bourbon News called him 'the brute' and described the mob as 'not to be outdone.' The Copiah Signal's report stood apart in noting Sarver's 'fair character' alongside the details of the hanging. The Hopkinsville South Kentuckian gave the case a line among its state news, and the Puget Sound Weekly Argus repeated it on March 17. Every report found treated the accusation as established and named no member of the mob.

reader.title: Lynching of Bob Sarver
bases: A mob took Sarver from officers and hanged him for an alleged attempted rape (A15, A18, A13).
Sarver was hanged by a mob of about 75 men who took him from officers, without trial, as punishment for an alleged attempted rape of a white girl (A15, A18, A1); three men were arrested for it (A20).
The Nashville wire (A3), the Stark County Democrat (A13), the Copiah Signal (A15) and the Bourbon News (A18) give separately worded accounts that agree on the seizure from officers and the hanging.

accounts.label: Nashville wire (Associated Press)
accounts.gist: Bob Sarver, colored, was lynched at Franklin, Ky., the night of March 6 for an attempt to rape a 16-year-old white girl named Ruly; no other detail.

accounts.label: Stark County Democrat brief
accounts.gist: The attempt was on 'Sina Ruley' the previous Friday; her screams brought help and he escaped but was arrested Monday, and on the way to jail a crowd stopped the train at Franklin and hanged him from a tree.

accounts.label: Nashville report in the Copiah Signal
accounts.gist: About 75 armed, mounted men took him from guards taking him to Bowling Green for safety, carried him to the spot of the alleged attempt about 20 miles from Franklin, and hanged him by the road; a coroner's jury found death at the hands of unknown persons.

accounts.label: Bourbon News account
accounts.gist: He hid in a thicket six miles northwest of Franklin, seized the girl and threatened her with a knife until woodcutters came; after his capture, authorities put him on a train to escape a gathering mob, which entered the car with revolvers and hanged him at the scene.

accounts.label: Memphis Appeal 'Tennessee News' item
accounts.gist: Three men were arrested for taking Sarver from the officers at Franklin and awaited trial, with public sentiment in their favor.

framing.detail: The Memphis Public Ledger headed the wire 'Served Him Right'.
The Las Vegas Daily Gazette headed it 'Rape Fiend Lynched' and the Tombstone Epitaph 'Lynched for Rape'.
The Evening Star and New-York Tribune ran it as 'A Colored Man Lynched'; Lancaster and Yankton papers ran it among crime briefs.
The Stark County Democrat called him 'the fiend' and the girl 'bright young'; the Bourbon News called him 'the brute' and the mob 'indignant'.
The Copiah Signal's report described an expert hangman's knot but also noted he was about 18 and 'had a fair character in the neighborhood'.
The Memphis Daily Appeal reported the arrest of three 'gentlemen' and that public sentiment favored them, without comment.

conflicts.note: Sarver is the spelling in most reports, including the Kentucky papers; the others look like telegraph variants of the same name.
All seem to name one girl; the Hopkinsville paper gives 'Miss Tennie Ruby'.
